content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, the Ancient of Days is understood as a symbolic depiction of God (typically God the Father) as the eternal, sovereign Judge — an aged, white-haired figure enthroned in glory, whose 'ancientness' signifies eternal pre-existence, unchanging wisdom, supreme authority, and the right to judge the kingdoms of the world and vindicate the saints.","primary_basis":["Daniel 7:9-10 (the Ancient of Days takes his seat; clothing white as snow, hair like pure wool; thrones set, court sits in judgment, books opened)","Daniel 7:13-14 (one like a son of man comes with the clouds and is presented before the Ancient of Days, receiving everlasting dominion)","Daniel 7:21-22 (the Ancient of Days comes and judgment is given in favor of the saints of the Most High)","Psalm 90:2 and Psalm 102:24-27 (God's eternity, often cited as background for the 'ancient' imagery)","Revelation 1:13-14 (hair white like wool, like snow — cited both to connect the imagery to deity and, in some traditions, to identify the figure with Christ)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The Ancient of Days as God the Father specifically, distinct from the Son of Man (Christ) who is presented before him — a proto-Trinitarian reading in which Daniel 7 depicts two divine persons.","basis":["Daniel 7:13-14","Matthew 26:64 and Mark 14:62 (Jesus applying the Son of Man coming with clouds to himself)","Acts 7:55-56"],"prominence":"dominant"},{"meaning":"The Ancient of Days identified with Christ himself (the Son), especially in Eastern Orthodox theology and iconography, on the grounds that Old Testament theophanies are appearances of the pre-incarnate Logos and that Revelation 1:14 applies the white-hair imagery to the risen Christ.","basis":["Revelation 1:13-16","John 1:18 (no one has seen the Father)","Daniel 7:9 read alongside Rev 1:14; supported by patristic and conciliar tradition (e.g., decisions associated with the Quinisext Council and later Russian church debates on icons)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"A historical-critical reading: the imagery derives from ancient Near Eastern (especially Ugaritic/Canaanite) depictions of the aged high god El presiding over the divine council, adapted by the author of Daniel to portray Israel's God as cosmic judge.","basis":["Daniel 7:9-10 compared with Ugaritic texts describing El as 'father of years' with grey hair, enthroned in council","Psalm 82:1 (God presiding in the divine council) as comparative background"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Latter-day Saint (Mormon) interpretation identifying the Ancient of Days as Adam, the oldest and 'most ancient' of the human family, who will preside at a great council at Adam-ondi-Ahman before Christ's return.","basis":["Daniel 7:9-14 as read through Doctrine and Covenants 27:11; 116; 138:38 and teachings of Joseph Smith"],"prominence":"rare"},{"meaning":"Some interpreters (including certain Jehovah's Witness and unitarian readings, and some older Jewish interpretation) stress that the Ancient of Days is simply Jehovah/the one God, with the Son of Man as a subordinate, non-divine figure (Messiah, or collectively the saints/Israel).","basis":["Daniel 7:13-14, 18, 27 (the kingdom given to 'the people of the saints of the Most High,' supporting a collective reading of the son of man)","Daniel 7:22"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"The term appears only in Daniel 7 (verses 9, 13, 22). There is broad, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox, and Jewish interpretation that the Ancient of Days represents God as the eternal enthroned Judge; the live interpretive dispute is not over whether the figure is divine but over which divine person is in view (Father vs. Son) and how the imagery relates to its ancient Near Eastern background. Western art and theology overwhelmingly treat the figure as the Father; Eastern iconographic tradition frequently identifies him with Christ. The LDS identification with Adam is a well-documented but confessionally isolated reading. Because the assignment of Daniel 7:22 grammar is ambiguous (whether the Ancient of Days 'comes' or judgment is given 'to'/'for' the saints), a few interpreters blur the distinction between the Ancient of Days and the Son of Man, which fuels the Christological identification."}
